headline: Final Day at Big 5: The Questions the Show Has Not Answered
deck: Four days of exhibits and sessions have settled what is being sold. They have not settled who will install it, who will verify it, or who will still be here in five years.
excerpt: Big 5 Construct Saudi closes on Wednesday after four days at the Riyadh Front Exhibition & Conference Center. The show has been clear about products and much less clear about the constraints that decide whether they get used: workforce, verification, procurement data and the durability of localisation.
content:
Big 5 Construct Saudi closes on Wednesday evening, and the halls have done what a good trade show does. More than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries have made it possible to compare products side by side, and a CPD-certified conference programme has put developers, contractors and consultants in front of an audience for four days. What the week has not resolved is the set of constraints sitting underneath all of it. Four questions are leaving Riyadh unanswered.

The first is who installs and maintains any of this. The Kingdom's construction workforce is not small: the General Authority for Statistics recorded roughly 3.4 million people working in the sector in its fourth-quarter 2025 labour force survey, with around 92 per cent of them non-Saudi. But headcount is not the constraint. Skill is. The products on this floor assume commissioning engineers, controls technicians, specialist quantity surveyors and supervisors who can hold a modern specification, and those are the roles that stay vacant longest. Nothing exhibited this week creates one of them.

That question has become sharper rather than softer, because the hiring surge has cooled. Construction hiring in the Kingdom has slowed to single-digit growth as giga-project ambitions are recalibrated and developers demand more certainty before adding headcount. A slower market is a reasonable moment to train people. It is also, historically, the moment training budgets get cut.

The second question is verification. The most encouraging thing about this week has been the quality of buyer questions — certification, tested performance, lifecycle cost, warranty scope, local support, spare parts, real references. The discouraging part is that a buyer asking those questions on a stand has almost no way to check the answers before an order is placed. Certificates cover configurations that are not always the configuration on offer. Performance data comes from test conditions that may not resemble a Riyadh summer. There is no shared registry a Saudi contractor can interrogate. The market has developed the right instinct and has not yet developed the infrastructure to act on it.

The third question is procurement data, which was the theme running through the programme's leadership sessions on digital transparency and supply-chain resilience. Saudi Arabia has done the platform work: public tendering has been consolidated onto Etimad, and the great majority of government procurement now runs through digital channels. What is still missing is the operational layer beneath the tender — actual lead times for a specific item from a specific plant, real stock held inside the Kingdom, the status of a submittal, the second source if the first slips. Software does not create that data. Suppliers do, and only if somebody makes it a contract condition.

The fourth question is whether localisation survives a cost squeeze. Localisation has been the strongest single message of the week, and Saudi manufacturers on this floor have made a coherent case for it that does not rest on price: shorter lead times, technical support in the same time zone, capacity that can be inspected, compliance with Saudi requirements. That argument holds while award volumes are high. The test comes when a contractor is squeezed on a fixed-price package and an imported alternative lands cheaper. Nothing at this show tells us which way that goes.

None of these is a criticism of the event. A trade show is a place where an industry displays what it has, and this one has displayed a great deal. But the gap between what is available in these halls and what is actually installed, verified, staffed and maintained on Saudi sites is the real story of the next few years, and it will be reported somewhere other than an exhibition floor.
author: Mo Qureshi
seoTitle: Big 5 Saudi's Final Day: Four Unanswered Questions
seoDescription: As Big 5 Construct Saudi closes, workforce skills, product verification, procurement data and the durability of localisation remain unresolved.
